11889:
Psalm 82 is only eight verses long, but it is one of the most argued-over passages in the Old Testament. God takes his place in a gathering called the 'congregation of God' (adat-el) and judges in the middle of the elohim, a Hebrew word that usually means 'God' or 'gods' but can occasionally refer to other powerful figures. He accuses them of judging unjustly and favouring the wicked, demands justice for the poor and fatherless, then pronounces: 'I have said, Ye are gods; and all of you are children of the most High. But ye shall die like men, and fall like one of the princes.' The psalm ends with a prayer: 'Arise, O God, judge the earth: for thou shalt inherit all nations.'

Three readings have a long history. Many modern scholars, and the divine-council view popular among evangelicals, read the 'gods' as heavenly beings who were meant to govern the nations and failed. A long Jewish and Christian tradition reads them as human rulers and judges, who exercise God's authority and can be called 'gods' because of their office. A rabbinic reading links the verse to Israel at Mount Sinai: when Israel received the Torah it was like the immortal angels, but by sinning with the golden calf it fell back into mortality.

The question matters partly because Jesus quotes Ps 82:6 when accused of blasphemy (John 10:34-36). How his argument works depends on whom the psalm addressed.
11890: Heavenly beings of the divine council
11891:
On this reading, Psalm 82 pictures a heavenly courtroom. God (Elohim, here standing for Yahweh) rises in the 'assembly of El' and passes sentence on the other elohim, divine beings to whom he had given responsibility for the nations. They have ruled unjustly, letting the poor be crushed, and so they will lose their immortality and 'die like men'. The psalm ends with a prayer that God himself will take over the nations they misgoverned.

This is the majority view in modern critical scholarship, from Hermann Gunkel and Hans-Joachim Kraus to many recent commentators, and it is central to the evangelical divine-council theology popularised by Michael Heiser. Defenders note the close parallels with the council of El in the Ugaritic texts, with Ps 89:5-7 and with Deut 32:8-9 in its Qumran form. They also note that it was already a Jewish reading before Christ: the Qumran Melchizedek scroll pictures a heavenly figure judging among the elohim using Ps 82:1. Christian defenders read the psalm as part of a biblical story in which rebellious powers are disarmed by Christ and the nations are reclaimed (Col 2:15; Rev 11:15).

11934:
This reading takes the 'gods' to be human judges, kings and magistrates. In Israel judges acted for God: bringing a case before them was bringing it 'before God' (Exod 22:8-9, where the KJV and older Jewish tradition translate elohim as 'the judges'). Because they carried God's authority, they could be called 'gods' and 'children of the most High', just as Moses was made 'a god to Pharaoh' (Exod 7:1). Psalm 82 is a prophetic rebuke: God stands among Israel's rulers, condemns their corrupt justice, and reminds them that for all their title they are mortal and will fall.

The view has deep roots in Jewish interpretation (the Aramaic Targum renders the scene in terms of judges, and Rashi follows it) and became standard in Christian commentary from the Reformation onward, through Calvin, Matthew Henry and Spurgeon. Its defenders stress the psalm's ethical content, which concerns orphans, the poor and bribery, and they read Jesus' quotation in John 10 as a straightforward lesser-to-greater argument: if Scripture calls human judges 'gods' because God's word appointed them, how much more can the one sent by the Father call himself God's Son.

11977:
A third reading, found in rabbinic literature, connects Psalm 82 with Israel's experience at Mount Sinai. When Israel received the Torah and said 'we will do, and be obedient' (Exod 24:7), God declared them 'gods' and 'children of the most High': in the rabbinic telling, they were freed from the power of death and became like the angels. But when they made the golden calf (Exod 32), they lost that status, and God said, 'you shall die like men', that is, like Adam, who also lost life through disobedience. The Babylonian Talmud (Avodah Zarah 5a) gives this interpretation, and later midrash develops it.

Some New Testament scholars, especially Jerome Neyrey, argue that this reading explains John 10:34-36 best. Jesus defines the 'gods' as 'them to whom the word of God came', which fits Israel receiving God's word at Sinai. His argument is then: if Israel was called 'gods' because it received the word, how much more the one who is himself the Word (John 1:1, 14), consecrated and sent by the Father. Early Christian writers such as Irenaeus developed a related idea, applying 'you are gods' to all who receive adoption through the Word, which became part of the Eastern Christian teaching on deification (theosis).
